auraIntro: Explorer, Andromeda briefing loaded. Review the metrics for our nearest major galactic neighbor.
overview: The Andromeda Galaxy (Messier 31) is a massive spiral galaxy located approximately 2.5 million light-years from Earth. It is the largest galaxy in our Local Group.
formation: Assembled through past galactic collisions approximately 10 billion years ago.
structure: Classic spiral galaxy with a double nucleus containing a supermassive black hole.
discoveryHistory: Cataloged by Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi in 964 CE as a 'small cloud'.
observationTips: Visible to the naked eye as a fuzzy smudge under dark skies; stunning through binoculars.
funFacts: Andromeda contains over 1 trillion stars—more than twice as many as the Milky Way.
It is traveling toward our galaxy at 110 kilometers per second.

cards.title: Messier 31 Overview
cards.subtitle: Colossus of the Local Group
cards.body: Spanning over 220,000 light-years, Andromeda is the largest galaxy in the Local Group. It hosts over 1 trillion stars and is surrounded by a swarm of satellite dwarf galaxies.

cards.title: Formation & Ancient Mergers
cards.subtitle: Cosmic Collision History
cards.body: Studies indicate Andromeda experienced a major merger approximately 2 to 3 billion years ago, shaping its prominent stellar halo and outer gas rings.
bulletPoints: Constructed from two smaller proto-galaxies that collided between 5 and 9 billion years ago.
Outer disk exhibits a subtle warp caused by gravitational tugs from M32 and M110.
Enormous gas halo extends halfway to the Milky Way.

visualPlaceholder.title: Galactic Collision Simulation
visualPlaceholder.caption: Hydrodynamic computer model simulating galactic merger physics.

cards.title: Double Nucleus & Stellar Halo
cards.subtitle: P1 and P2 Central Supermassive Core
cards.body: Hubble observations revealed Andromeda has a double optical nucleus (P1 and P2). The core houses a supermassive black hole with a mass of 100 million Suns.
bulletPoints: P1 and P2 cores result from an eccentric ring of aging blue stars orbiting the black hole.
Extensive stellar stream in halo represents remnants of disrupted satellite galaxies.
Contains over 460 globular clusters, including Mayall II (G1).

visualPlaceholder.title: Hubble Core Spectrograph
visualPlaceholder.caption: Ultra-deep UV and optical resolution of the central nucleus.

cards.title: Historical Discovery & Edwin Hubble
cards.subtitle: Unlocking the Extragalactic Universe
cards.body: In 1923, Edwin Hubble identified Cepheid variable stars in Andromeda, proving for the first time that M31 was an independent galaxy far beyond the Milky Way.
bulletPoints: First recorded by Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi in 964 CE as a 'little cloud'.
Charles Messier cataloged it as M31 in 1764.
Hubble's 1923 discovery settled the famous 'Great Debate' about the scale of the cosmos.

visualPlaceholder.title: Hubble 1923 VAR Glass Plate
visualPlaceholder.caption: Historic photographic plate where Edwin Hubble wrote 'VAR!' discovering Cepheid variables.

cards.title: The Milky Way - Andromeda Collision
cards.subtitle: Inseparable Cosmic Destiny
cards.body: Andromeda is moving toward the Milky Way at 110 km/s. In approximately 4.5 billion years, both giants will collide and merge to form a massive elliptical galaxy.
bulletPoints: Stellar distances are so vast that individual stars will likely pass each other without colliding.
Interstellar gas clouds will compress, triggering intense starburst activity.
The Solar System will likely be flung into a new outer orbit in the merged galaxy.
